title: Trigonometry: Choosing Law of Sines or Law of Cosines Assessment
description: Show decision-chart reasoning for mixed oblique triangle problems, then choose the correct first law.

questions.question: Which given case starts with Law of Cosines because no opposite side-angle pair is known?
options: AAS
ASA
SAS
SSA
questions.explanation: SAS gives two sides and the included angle. There is no complete opposite pair, so Law of Cosines is the first law.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, A = 36 degrees, B = 81 degrees, and c = 18. What is the best first move?
options: Use Law of Cosines to find side a
Find C, then use Law of Sines
Use Law of Cosines to find angle C
Use the ambiguous-case height test
questions.explanation: Two angles and one side are known. First find C = 180 degrees - 36 degrees - 81 degrees, then use Law of Sines with the complete pair C and c.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, a = 8, b = 13, and C = 47 degrees. Which expression is the correct first setup?
options: sin C / c = sin 47 degrees / 13
C = 180 degrees - 8 degrees - 13 degrees
questions.explanation: This is SAS with included angle C between sides a and b, so the Law of Cosines finds the opposite side c.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, a = 9, b = 14, and c = 16. Which angle is a sensible first angle to find, and why?
options: A, because it is listed first
B, because b is between a and c
C, because it is opposite the longest side
Any angle using Law of Sines immediately
questions.explanation: For SSS, Law of Cosines finds an angle first. Choosing C is sensible because side c = 16 is longest, so angle C should be largest and easy to check.

questions.question: SSA problems should start with Law of Cosines because two sides are known.
questions.explanation: SSA has a known angle opposite a known side, so Law of Sines is the usual first law. However, the ambiguous case must be considered.

questions.question: A learner writes: 'A = 52 degrees, a = 17, b = 12 gives a complete pair A and a.' What should the learner choose first?
options: Law of Sines, with an SSA ambiguity check
Law of Cosines, because b is known
Triangle angle sum first
No law is possible
questions.explanation: The data is SSA. The complete pair A and a makes Law of Sines available, but SSA requires checking whether the measurements make one or two possible triangles.

questions.question: Which note best explains why ASA starts with Law of Sines?
options: ASA always has three known sides after drawing a diagram.
Two known angles let you find the third angle, creating an opposite side-angle pair.
The included side must be the longest side.
Law of Cosines cannot use angles.
questions.explanation: ASA gives two angles, so the third angle is found by subtraction. Then the known side can be matched with its opposite angle for Law of Sines.

questions.question: Write the three-letter case only: two sides and a non-included angle.
questions.explanation: Two sides and a non-included angle form the SSA case.

questions.question: Write the three-letter case only: three side lengths are known.
questions.explanation: When all three side lengths are known, the case is SSS.

questions.question: Decision chart notes: In triangle ABC, A = 41 degrees, B = 74 degrees, and a = 15. State the case, complete pair, first law, and reason.
questions.correctAnswer: The case is AAS. A complete pair is A = 41 degrees with a = 15. Use the Law of Sines first because a known side is paired with its opposite known angle, and the third angle can be found from the angle sum.
questions.explanation: A complete answer identifies AAS, names A and a as the complete pair, selects Law of Sines, and gives the opposite-pair reason.

questions.question: Decision chart notes: In triangle ABC, b = 10, c = 18, and A = 67 degrees. State the case, whether a complete pair is known, first law, and reason.
questions.correctAnswer: The case is SAS because angle A is included between sides b and c. No complete opposite side-angle pair is known at first. Use the Law of Cosines first to find side a.
questions.explanation: A strong response recognizes that b and c meet at angle A, so the data is SAS. Since there is no complete pair, Law of Cosines is the correct first law.
